From Freshers' Week to First Exams: 校园生活
一个内向新生的第一学期:从迎新周的喧嚣,到宿舍、社团与答疑课,最终找到属于自己的学习节奏。
B2

Nobody warns you that freshers' week is a marathon performed at sprint pace. For seven days the campus hums like a hive: wristbands, queueing curry, and conversations that all begin with the same three questions — what do you study, where are you from, and which halls are you in? I am, by nature, the person who leaves parties early, so I approached the whole carnival with a private dread. On the second night I stood at the edge of the student union bar holding a drink I did not want, rehearsing an exit line, when a girl in a dinosaur costume asked whether I had signed up for the baking society yet. I had not. I signed up on the spot, mostly to have something to say, and it turned out to be the single best decision of my first term.

Halls of residence deserve their strange reputation. Twenty strangers share one kitchen, and the kitchen becomes a parliament where every human habit is legislated: whose milk this is, why the frying pan lives in the sink, what hour noise must die. My flatmates ranged from a nurse who woke at five to a drummer who apparently did not sleep at all. For the first fortnight we were aggressively polite; by the third we had negotiated a rota and a shared shelf; by December we were a weird, bickering family. Living in halls teaches domestic diplomacy faster than any course teaches its subject, and the skill outlasts the module marks.

Academic life, meanwhile, restarted from zero. A university lecture is not a school lesson: two hundred students, fifty minutes, a professor who will not notice whether you listen. In week one I transcribed every word like a court stenographer and understood almost nothing. The turning point came from a second-year who glanced at my notes and said one devastating sentence: "You're writing down what she says, not what it means." From then on I prepared before each lecture, went in with three questions, and used the hour to argue with the slides in the margins. My notes shrank to a third of the size and tripled in usefulness.

The tutorial saved me in ways I did not expect. Ten students, one tutor, one essay to defend every fortnight — it is a format designed to expose exactly the gaps a lecture hides. My first tutorial essay came back bleeding with red ink and one comment that still stings: "Confidently wrong throughout." Devastating, but fair. The fortnightly rhythm forced me to read properly, to finish a draft five days early, and to arrive knowing which paragraph I could not defend. By term's end I had learned to love tutorials precisely because they were uncomfortable; discomfort, it turns out, is the feeling of a weakness being found in time.

Then January brought the first exams, and with them a lesson in humility. My revision began optimistically with a colour-coded plan and collapsed within four days into highlighter anarchy. What rescued me was the reading list — or rather, rereading it properly. Each course had listed three chapters per week, and I had treated them as optional garnish all term. Facing two hundred pages of backlog, I discovered that the examiners asked about ideas, not page numbers, and that one well-understood argument was worth more than ten half-remembered quotations. I rewrote my plan around ideas: for each topic, one page in my own words, closed book, then checked against the texts.

On results day I passed everything — not at the top of the year, but comfortably, and with marks I could explain. Walking out of the student union with my flatmates, still arguing about the frying pan, I realised how much had changed since the girl in the dinosaur costume found me hovering at the edge of things. The trick nobody tells freshers is simple: say yes to one silly society, rewrite your notes into meaning, defend an essay out loud every fortnight, and treat the reading list as the syllabus in disguise. Freshers' week ends; what you build during it, quietly, in the following ten weeks, is what actually stays — the flatmates who become witnesses to your worst cooking, the society that rescues your weekends, and the first fragile sense that this enormous place might, in the end, be manageable.
